papers.abstract: Diffusion and flow-based generative models support high-quality image, audio, and video synthesis. Sampling can require dozens to hundreds of denoiser evaluations, with each pass becoming more expensive as resolution, video length, or model size increases. This cost affects latency and energy use in interactive and edge applications. We examine four approaches to accelerating inference: distillation, consistency training, sampling methods, and denoiser design. We express training objectives, transition maps, and numerical updates in a common notation to compare changes to the learning target, the sampling trajectory, and the work performed within each denoiser pass. Published image and video benchmarks illustrate the quality--cost trade-offs of one- and few-step generation, the interaction between solvers and timestep schedules, the effect of feature caching, and the difference between first-frame latency and sustained streaming throughput. We close with open problems in visual-native architectures and post-compression distillation, solver-aware few-step training, and semantic trajectory alignment with factorized distribution matching.
bullets: Diffusion sampling can require dozens to hundreds of denoiser evaluations, creating latency and energy costs that grow with resolution, video length, and model size.
The survey compares distillation, consistency training, sampling methods, and denoiser design using a common framework for learning targets, sampling trajectories, and per-step computation.
Published image and video benchmarks examine one- and few-step quality–cost trade-offs, solver and timestep-schedule interactions, feature caching, and streaming performance.
Open questions include visual-native architectures, post-compression distillation, solver-aware few-step training, and semantic trajectory alignment.

papers.tldr: A unified analysis of diffusion acceleration methods clarifies how they trade off generation quality, sampling cost, and latency across image, audio, and video synthesis.

papers.abstract: Real-world evaluation of generalist robot policies is bottlenecked by manual resets, human grading, and small fixed task suites with limited diagnostic coverage. We present ScaleEvals, a scalable reset-free protocol that evaluates policies through continuous physical play across a robot fleet. A VLM AutoPrompter generates scene-grounded tasks with difficulty estimates, language prompts, and skill tags, enabling performance analysis across diverse rollouts. A VLM AutoGrader assesses task progress, achieving 90.7% agreement with human graders. Scores are aggregated via a soft-win Bradley-Terry model, while tag-stratified ANOVA provides interpretable capability diagnostics. Across 3,000+ physical autonomous rollouts on DROID and YAM, ScaleEvals achieves 23.0 net rollouts/hr per station while reducing active human labor by 98%. By ranking five SOTA generalist policies, ScaleEvals correlates with held-out manual evaluation ranking on DROID (r=0.94, rho=0.90, p=0.018), and remains internally consistent on a second embodiment, YAM (r=0.839, rho=0.80). Beyond aggregate rankings, we observe behavioral compositionality: recombining verb-, skill-, and object-conditioned evidence predicts policy order on unseen prompts. Across 10 tasks and 240 prospective physical rollouts, we recover three-policy orderings of 96% pairwise concordance, demonstrating ScaleEvals can predict not just which policy leads, but where rankings reverse.
bullets: Addresses evaluation bottlenecks caused by manual resets, human grading, and narrow fixed task suites.
Uses VLM-generated, scene-grounded tasks with difficulty estimates, language prompts, and skill tags during continuous robot play.
Combines VLM grading, soft-win Bradley–Terry aggregation, and tag-stratified ANOVA for capability diagnostics.
Across 3,000+ rollouts, achieves 23.0 net rollouts/hour per station and reduces active human labor by 98%; VLM grading agrees with humans 90.7% of the time.
Ranks five generalist policies consistently with manual evaluations and predicts unseen-prompt ranking reversals through compositional behavioral evidence.

papers.abstract: Object manipulation in the dynamic real world requires understanding how the environment functions and evolves, and acting accordingly. Existing benchmarks, however, do not adequately address these needs. Physics-oriented benchmarks evaluate predictive fidelity but not closed-loop action. Dynamic robotic manipulation benchmarks often use simplified, physically implausible object motions, limiting evaluation of reasoning and action under realistic dynamics. Evaluation is also typically synchronized, freezing the environment during inference and making computation time irrelevant to task outcomes. To this end, we propose RoboDyna, a benchmark for evaluating the physical understanding and action capabilities of manipulation policies in dynamic scenes. RoboDyna comprises 20 conceptual dynamic tasks spanning five capability categories, with simple objects and minimal scene clutter, under a two-factor difficulty design, and 10 household tasks that instantiate the same capabilities in visually and semantically richer simulated real-world environments. RoboDyna provides 3,500 expert demonstrations, paired synchronous and asynchronous evaluation protocols, metrics for task success and partial completion, and interactive tools for human baseline evaluation. Evaluating vision-language-action models and a world-action model across 5.4K episodes, we find that all policies achieve success rates below 20%, revealing substantial limitations in dynamic manipulation. The world-action model captures simple physical dynamics but struggles with complex interactions, and its prediction fidelity does not consistently align with task success. Sync-async comparisons show that inference latency flips 5-12% of episode outcomes while changing average success rates by at most 3%. Human baselines substantially outperform all policies under matched conditions. Project page: https://robodyna.github.io/robodyna/
bullets: Covers 20 conceptual dynamic tasks across five capabilities and 10 richer household tasks.
Includes 3,500 expert demonstrations, synchronous and asynchronous protocols, partial-completion metrics, and human-baseline tools.
Evaluations across 5.4K episodes show all tested policies achieve below 20% success, while humans substantially outperform them.
World-action models capture simple dynamics but struggle with complex interactions; prediction fidelity does not consistently predict task success.
Inference latency changes 5–12% of episode outcomes, though average success rates shift by at most 3%.

papers.abstract: Logical Anomaly Detection (LAD) requires verifying whether all category-specific constraints, such as object counts, pairing relations, and measurement ranges, are satisfied by a query image given only a few normal references. Recent LAD methods based on Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) formulate this as checklist verification, decomposing the decision into independent textual checks. This decomposition, however, is text-only. Every item still reads the same unmodified query image, so the LVLM must extract different forms of visual evidence from one raw image. We identify this text-image mismatch as a constraint-specific perception gap, the source of two failure modes: instance conflation for binding constraints and scale drift for calibration constraints. To diagnose whether these failures stem from insufficient reasoning or insufficient perception, we compare textual reasoning guides and visual perception guides in a training-free setting. Our analysis shows that reasoning over the same image provides little benefit, whereas adapting the visual input to each constraint substantially improves verification accuracy. Based on this finding, we propose CASCADE, a training-free framework that extends checklist decomposition using constraint-specific visual scaffolds. We further introduce CASCADE++, which adapts these scaffolds at the object level by deriving their configurations from the constraint structure and reference distribution. Across MVTec-LOCO and VID-AD, CASCADE++ surpasses the full-shot state of the art by 3.9 AUROC points with only three references, and improves over the strongest VID-AD baseline by 11.4, transferring across multiple LVLM backbones without any training.
bullets: LAD checks category-specific constraints such as counts, pairings, and measurement ranges using only a few normal references.
Text-only checklist methods suffer from a constraint-specific perception gap, causing instance conflation and scale drift.
CASCADE adds constraint-specific visual scaffolds; CASCADE++ further adapts them at the object level using constraint structure and reference distributions.

The training-free approach transfers across multiple LVLM backbones and improves results on MVTec-LOCO and VID-AD, including a 3.9-point AUROC gain over full-shot state of the art with three references.
The study suggests visual adaptation, rather than additional reasoning over the same image, is the key improvement.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Method comparison between the baseline and CASCADE. Both methods use checklist generator and checklist verifier for verdicts. Unlike the baseline, ours overlays a constraint-specific scaffold on the query image, so each constraint is verified with an adapted visual input.

Fig. 1: Checklist verification on a raw query versus a scaffolded query—per-instance coloring for counting, an object-anchored grid for measurement. Both are the same image verified against the same checklist item, and both violate their constraint, yet only the scaffolded query yields the correct verdict. The Measurement condition is defined by the K = 3 references shown in the band rather than stated explicitly (Section VII-B).

Fig. 5: Comparison of within-image and cross-image length readings on a scale probe. We render a bar of fixed true length with a ground truth of 320 px and read its length from the LVLM. A within-image reading repeats the same image, while a cross-image reading spans separate renderings of the same length.

Fig. 6: Comparison of readout strategies on a range-membership probe. Balanced Accuracy across violation margins for three VLM backbones. A test bar is judged against the range of K=3 references, calibrated in code as in CASCADE, so the backbone reads only the test: Comparison sees the references too and answers directly, Pixel reports raw pixels, Patch units of an imagined 12×12 grid, and the object-centric readout an index off a scale drawn on the bar; the last three are rangechecked in code.

Fig. 3: Comparison of textual reasoning and visual perception guides. Bars show balanced accuracy on a binding constraint for Counting and the average over calibration constraints for Measurement, with the dashed lines indicating the text-only baselines. Each overlay is applied to both constraint types, not only the one it was designed for.

Fig. 4: Comparison of raw and per-instance colored images on a counting probe. We query the count of n identical circles on a blank canvas, varying only n. Raw-image accuracy (red) collapses past n ≈ 10, while distinctly coloring each circle (gray) keeps it far higher throughout.

papers.abstract: Robots operating in the real world are inherently subject to partial observability, particularly in multi-robot collaboration, where individual observations may be insufficient for effective task execution. A key challenge is leveraging complementary observations from partner robots to support collaborative decision-making. We argue that information sharing should go beyond passively transmitting raw observations or generic visual features. Instead, robots should selectively encode task-relevant information according to task objectives and execution progress. To this end, we propose a task-oriented active context sharing framework that transforms robot observations into compact representations, preserving critical information under constrained communication budgets. The framework adopts a two-stage training paradigm. In the first stage, onboard observations and task instructions are jointly encoded into compact context representations. Task-oriented future prediction and soft task-progress correspondence learning guide this collaboration-agnostic compression, preserving information about task objectives and execution progress. In the second stage, the learned representations are integrated into a pretrained Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policy, enabling bidirectional context exchange. Each robot combines complementary partner information with local observations to guide action generation. Action supervision jointly refines the context representations and policy, aligning information sharing with collaborative decision-making. Controlled experiments demonstrate substantial performance gains under constrained communication budgets, while three real-world experiments validate the framework in complex dual-robot tasks. These results highlight a shift from passive visual transmission toward active, task-oriented context sharing that directly supports collaborative decision-making.
bullets: Addresses partial observability in multi-robot tasks where each robot’s view is insufficient.
Compresses observations using task instructions, future prediction, and task-progress correspondence learning.
Integrates the learned context into a pretrained Vision-Language-Action policy for bidirectional information exchange.
Action supervision jointly refines context representations and policy toward collaborative decision-making.
Controlled and real-world dual-robot experiments show gains under constrained communication budgets.

figures.caption: Figure 1 | Overview of the two-stage active context sharing framework. In Stage 1, multicamera observations and task instructions are compressed into shared context, optimized through weighted future visual feature prediction and soft-label contrastive learning. In Stage 2, robots bidirectionally exchange local context and condition their VLA policies on shared context to generate continuous actions for collaborative decision-making.

Figure 2 | Soft Task-Progress Correspondence Learning. For each observation, augmented views are encoded by the task-conditioned context encoder and treated as positive pairs. Taskand progress-based affinities define the similarity matrix for contrastive learning, promoting cross-view consistency, inter-task discriminability, and intra-task temporal continuity.
Figure 3 | Representative rollouts of designed collaborative tasks. Keyframes highlight critical moments of inter-robot context sharing during task execution.

Figure 4 | Representative rollouts of more collaborative tasks. Keyframes highlight critical moments of inter-robot context sharing during task execution.

papers.tldr: A task-oriented active context-sharing framework helps robots selectively exchange compact, decision-relevant information for better collaboration under limited communication.

papers.abstract: Mamba is a neural network architecture that reduces computational complexity, and has been shown to be effective for 3D medical image segmentation. However, existing models still remain computationally expensive. We propose compressing Mamba by distillation while achieving competitive performance. Specifically, we demonstrate compression of a 139M-parameter SegMamba-V2 teacher into a lightweight TinyUNet3D student with about 0.96M parameters, achieving about 145$\times$ compression with a performance drop of just over one Dice point. We further investigate the utility of knowledge distillation in a range of data-labeling scenarios under identical experimental settings, and show that its advantage is most prominent when labeled data is scarce. To demonstrate the generalizability of our approach, experiments are conducted on three datasets: BraTS 2023, MSD Spleen and MSD Hippocampus. The code for TinyUNet3D is publicly available at: https://github.com/2802990u/tinyunet3d-dist-kd.
bullets: Compresses a 139M-parameter SegMamba-V2 teacher into a roughly 0.96M-parameter TinyUNet3D student.
Achieves about 145× parameter compression with a performance decrease of just over one Dice point.
Evaluates knowledge distillation across different labeling scenarios, finding its advantage is strongest with limited labeled data.
Demonstrates the approach on BraTS 2023, MSD Spleen, and MSD Hippocampus.
TinyUNet3D code is publicly available.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of the proposed framework, illustrating the distillation of knowledge from a large Mamba teacher model into an ultra-lightweight student architecture.

Fig. 2. Effect of training data size on KD using BraTS 2023 (100% = 876 training cases). Points are means over 3 seeds, and gains are paired by seed. Left: student test Dice (fraction) with and without DIST. Right: DIST gain over the no-KD student.
Fig. 3. Qualitative segmentation results across three 3D medical imaging datasets. The first row shows the ground truth slices while the second row shows the predicted scans.

Table 1. Comparison with SOTA methods on three datasets. Our results use a fixed held-out split, with checkpoints selected on a validation set and the test set scored once;student results are averaged over 3 seeds. Dice scores of published methods are taken from their papers (own protocols); the BraTS baselines (SegResNet, Swin UNETR-V2, SegMamba) are from Table 2 of [8]. papers.abstract: Mamba has the capability to capture global context in linear time for 3D medical image segmentation. However, existing methods employ Mamba with full-width directional scans at every resolution, keeping the model large (64-138M parameters and high FLOPs). We propose Grouped Multi-Directional (GMD) Mamba, a lightweight network based on the GMD scan that divides input channels $C$ into groups $G$ and flattens each group in different directions in one pass. This gives multi-directional context at $O(C^2/G)$ instead of $O(K \cdot C^2)$, where $K$ is the number of scan directions. Additionally, we employ Mamba only at the deepest encoder stages, resulting in 19.2M parameters. On BraTS2023, it achieves the best average Dice of 92.0% and the lowest HD95 of 2.7 at $\sim$1/7 the parameters of SegMamba-V2. For model validation, we also ran experiments on the MSD Spleen dataset, achieving competitive performance. The implementation details and code are publicly available at https://github.com/2802990u/GMD-Mamba.
bullets: Existing 3D Mamba segmenters use full-width scans at every resolution, leading to large models and high computational cost.
GMD scanning splits channels into groups and processes them in different directions in one pass, reducing scan complexity to O(C²/G).
Mamba is restricted to the deepest encoder stages, producing a 19.2M-parameter network.
On BraTS2023, GMD-Mamba reports 92.0% average Dice and 2.7 HD95, using about one-seventh the parameters of SegMamba-V2.
It also achieves competitive results on the MSD Spleen dataset; broader scope is limited to the reported datasets.

papers.abstract: DeepSearch LLM agents repeatedly search and carry retrieved sources into subsequent reasoning steps. This expanding context increases token consumption and latency, although many results do not contribute to later reasoning. We propose Query-Relevant Attention Entropy (QRAE), an online context compression method that uses sparse evidence-assessment heads to decide which intact retrieved chunks should persist across reasoning steps. It scores bounded candidate batches through paired prefills: a query-free control suppresses shared attention responses, while normalized entropy measures the breadth of the positive response within each chunk. High-scoring chunks enter a persistent evidence whitelist and are included in the reasoning context. Uncertain chunks remain outside the reasoning context but are retained in a candidate cache, where they can be retrieved for later reevaluation. QRAE requires neither an additional generative compression pass nor modification of the attention operator. Across multiple DeepSearch benchmarks and reasoning models, QRAE improves task success by an average of 2.35 percentage points and reduces end-to-end latency and reported token usage by an average of 30% and 45%, respectively. These benefits generalize to a model with nearly 100B parameters.
bullets: Targets context growth in iterative DeepSearch agents, where many retrieved sources are not useful for later reasoning.
Uses sparse evidence-assessment heads and paired prefills to score candidate chunks via normalized attention-response entropy.
Persists high-scoring chunks in an evidence whitelist; uncertain chunks remain in a cache for possible later reevaluation.
Across multiple benchmarks and reasoning models, it improves task success by 2.35 percentage points on average, while reducing latency by 30% and reported token usage by 45%.
The approach generalizes to a model with nearly 100B parameters and requires no extra generative compression pass or attention-operator changes.

papers.abstract: In this paper, we propose ThinkLocoManip, an agentic harness for legged loco-manipulation designed to tackle complex, long-horizon tasks in large-scale environments. Existing approaches typically follow either direct action generation or a plan-then-act paradigm, both of which can struggle with the generalization and error-recovery capabilities required for extended task execution. In contrast, ThinkLocoManip adopts an interleaved reasoning-and-acting paradigm, allowing the agent to continuously reason about its current state, execute actions, observe their outcomes, and adapt its strategy accordingly. Building on this paradigm, our agentic harness orchestrates a suite of specialized tools for perception, navigation, manipulation, and locomotion, enabling flexible composition of heterogeneous capabilities. Unlike existing robotic agentic harnesses, ThinkLocoManip explicitly incorporates locomotion as a tool domain for agent reasoning and execution. We further design a set of skills that explicitly account for both tool usage within each functional domain and coordination across domains, supporting effective execution of complex behaviors over long horizons. To tackle task failure during long-horizon interactions, we develop keyframe thinking mechanism to preserve critical execution context and support efficient error recovery. Extensive real-world experiments demonstrate that ThinkLocoManip substantially outperforms representative methods based on both direct action generation and plan-then-act paradigms across challenging long-horizon legged loco-manipulation tasks. Notably, ThinkLocoManip achieves a success rate of 77%, more than twice that of the strongest plan-then-act baseline (37.1%). Our experiments further validate the effectiveness of interleaved reasoning and acting, tool orchestration, and coordinated skill execution.
bullets: Targets the limited generalization and error recovery of direct-action and plan-then-act approaches.
Continuously reasons, acts, observes outcomes, and adapts its strategy during execution.
Orchestrates perception, navigation, manipulation, and locomotion tools, explicitly treating locomotion as a reasoning domain.
Uses coordinated cross-domain skills and keyframe thinking to preserve context and recover from failures.
Real-world experiments report a 77% success rate, versus 37.1% for the strongest plan-then-act baseline.

papers.abstract: Recent efforts have demonstrated the strong capabilities of Multimodal Large Reasoning Models (MLRMs) in geographic reasoning. By jointly analyzing subtle visual cues, these models can infer the locations of photos, thus enabling doxing even by non-expert adversaries. Existing defense methods struggle to balance the shareability of photos with effective protection, and often fail to sufficiently disrupt the implicit geo-evidence chains embedded in scene semantics. To this end, we propose GeoEdit, an adversarial de-evidencing framework for silent geoprivacy protection via image editing. Specifically, we apply minimal edits to high-risk evidence anchors in the image, thereby disrupting the underlying spatial reasoning chains while preserving overall scene semantics. We identify these anchors by combining structured knowledge with adversarially discovered geographic cues. To further navigate the large editing action space, we adopt a learnable policy to iteratively refine editing decisions, distilling successful trajectories into transferable natural-language insights for consistent and efficient editing. Evaluated on LifePhotoBench, GeoEdit achieves strong protection against 6 mainstream MLRMs, outperforming visual perturbation baselines by over 0.59 in image fidelity.
bullets: Targets implicit visual evidence chains that MLRMs use to infer photo locations.
Identifies geographic evidence anchors using structured knowledge and adversarially discovered cues.
Uses a learnable policy to iteratively refine edits and distill successful strategies into natural-language guidance.
On LifePhotoBench, protects against six mainstream MLRMs and exceeds visual-perturbation baselines by over 0.59 in image fidelity.

papers.abstract: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) deliver high-fidelity image and video generation, but inference requires many sequential model evaluations. Two acceleration strategies are increasingly important: model compression makes each evaluation cheaper, while adaptive inference avoids selected teacher computation through reuse, forecasting, or speculative execution. Their combination, however, is brittle: directly applying the evaluated adaptive methods to a compressed student can degrade quality, an observed failure mode we call the \textbf{Combination Gap}. We link this gap to a mismatch between pointwise distillation and short-horizon execution: a student trained at teacher states need not remain reliable when its own predictions are chained. We propose \textbf{TamedFlow}, which trains a compressed DiT for this deployed role through cross-architecture feature alignment, a near-identity Velocity Alignment Head, and randomized rollout supervision. At inference, a lightweight Learnable Trajectory Estimator routes completed drafts: accepted drafts bypass the teacher, while rejected drafts roll back and receive one teacher rescue step. Distilling DiT-XL/2 into DiT-B/2, TamedFlow reaches FID $2.58$ at $2.25\times$ measured speedup over DDIM-50 on ImageNet $256\times256$. Ablations support trajectory supervision, and routing controls favor LTE over random decisions at nearly matched latency. Evaluations on ImageNet $512\times512$, MS-COCO, and Latte/FaceForensics extend the empirical scope.
bullets: The work addresses quality degradation when adaptive inference methods are applied to compressed diffusion students.
It combines cross-architecture feature alignment, a near-identity Velocity Alignment Head, and randomized rollout supervision.
A Learnable Trajectory Estimator accepts completed drafts or triggers rollback with one teacher rescue step.
For DiT-XL/2 distilled to DiT-B/2, it reports FID 2.58 and a 2.25× measured speedup over DDIM-50 on ImageNet 256×256.
Additional evaluations cover higher-resolution ImageNet, MS-COCO, and Latte/FaceForensics; ablations support trajectory supervision and learned routing.

papers.abstract: Passive-wheel quadrupedal robots offer energy-efficient locomotion through leg-driven propulsion and momentum-driven gliding. However, navigation requires coordinating steering with intermittent propulsion and adapting push-glide timing to task demands. Velocity-tracking objectives may suppress the speed variations inherent in skating, discouraging efficient gliding. To address these challenges, we propose SkateNav, a unified skating-navigation framework based on reinforcement learning. A time-budgeted goal-reaching objective allows the policy to jointly learn steering, propulsion, and their temporal allocation. An adaptive skating cycle structures gliding, pushing, and recovery, while frequency modulation at every control step adjusts phase durations to navigation demands. Simulation experiments demonstrate higher average success rates and lower cost of transport than the evaluated planner-controller baselines, with ablations confirming the contributions of cycle structure and frequency adaptation. Real-world experiments demonstrate zero-shot transfer from simulation to a passive-wheel Mini Cheetah across cluttered indoor spaces, slopes, and paved outdoor surfaces. Supplementary videos are available on the project page: https://ktw1404.github.io/SkateNav/
bullets: Addresses the challenge of navigating with intermittent leg propulsion and momentum-driven gliding.
Uses a time-budgeted goal-reaching objective to jointly learn steering, propulsion, and their timing.
Introduces an adaptive skating cycle with per-step frequency modulation for gliding, pushing, and recovery.
Simulation results show higher average success rates and lower cost of transport than evaluated planner-controller baselines.
Transfers zero-shot to a passive-wheel Mini Cheetah across cluttered indoor areas, slopes, and paved outdoor surfaces.

papers.abstract: Dynamic object manipulation requires robots to anticipate target motion while replanning fast enough to avoid executing outdated actions. Existing approaches either rely on fast reactive control without an explicit future target state or encode anticipated motion only implicitly. World Action Models (WAMs) offer a promising alternative by coupling future visual prediction with action generation, but scene-level video objectives may underrepresent target dynamics that are critical for manipulation, while iterative video-action denoising introduces substantial latency. We present TrajWAM, a trajectory-guided world action model for efficient dynamic robotic manipulation. Our key insight is to explicitly ground future visual imagination in predicted target-object motion and use the resulting future representation to condition action generation, while preserving this anticipation pathway after acceleration. Given a short history of object masks, a history-conditioned motion predictor forecasts future masks encoding the target object's trajectory. A lightweight Trajectory ControlNet then steers a pretrained video model toward trajectory-consistent futures. The resulting future representation conditions an action expert to predict executable action chunks. To enable one-step inference without breaking this interface, we introduce a decoupled distillation scheme that combines distribution matching for the video backbone, Trajectory ControlNet realignment, and action rollout distillation to support accurate one-step action prediction conditioned on the compressed future representation. Comprehensive evaluations in simulation and the real world show that TrajWAM achieves state-of-the-art performance on dynamic object manipulation tasks while enabling efficient one-step video-action inference. Project page: https://kevingeng3.github.io/TrajWAM/.
bullets: Addresses the need to anticipate moving targets while replanning quickly enough to avoid stale actions.
Predicts future object masks from short mask histories to encode target motion explicitly.
Uses a lightweight Trajectory ControlNet to guide a pretrained video model toward trajectory-consistent future representations.
Conditions an action expert on these representations to generate executable action chunks.
Introduces decoupled distillation for efficient one-step video-action inference, with strong simulation and real-world results reported.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of TrajWAM. (a) Training pipeline. A language-conditioned segmentation model extracts the mask history of the target object, from which a motion predictor forecasts a sequence of future masks representing its anticipated trajectory. The predicted mask trajectory guides future-video generation through a Trajectory ControlNet, and the resulting trajectory-controlled video representation conditions the action branch through asymmetric video–action attention to predict an executable action chunk. (b) Inference pipeline. Target-object masks are updated online from incoming observations and maintained in a short history buffer. The predicted future mask trajectory guides the distilled one-step video model, whose future representation conditions the one-step action model for low-latency closed-loop control.

Fig. 8. Object-centric trajectory prediction on three DOMINO tasks and two real-world grasping sequences. Each row shows the current scene, four input masks, and four of the eight future predictions. Blue regions denote reference masks; orange contours denote predictions. Future overlays use the corresponding recorded RGB frames. References are dataset ground-truth masks for DOMINO and SAM3 segmentations for the real-world sequences. Time labels indicate offsets in source-video frames relative to t. All temporal panels within a row share a fixed crop; the current scene retains the full field of view.

Fig. 6. Qualitative comparison of real-world conveyor-belt grasping. Snapshots are shown at 1 s intervals from T = 0 to 4 s. TrajWAM conditions action generation on trajectory-guided future visual representations to anticipate target motion, successfully grasping and lifting the moving banana. In the illustrated trials, π0.5 and Fast-WAM fail to secure the object. Red crosses and the green check mark indicate grasp failure and success, respectively.

Fig. 3. Video distillation. (a) Video backbone distillation compresses the multi-step video generator into a fast generator using a frozen real-score function and a trainable fake-score function under distribution matching distillation. (b) ControlNet realignment adapts the Trajectory ControlNet to the frozen fast video model using latent reconstruction and diffusiondiscriminator objectives.

Fig. 4. Action rollout distillation. The slow teacher and fast student receive the same observation, language instruction, trajectory condition, and initial noises. The trainable fast action model is optimized to match the action chunk generated by the slow multi-step teacher.

Fig. 9. Video predictions on DOMINO training demonstrations. From top to bottom: Adjust Bottle, Click Bell, Move Pillbottle Pad, Place Bread Basket, and Place Object Scale. Each pair of rows shows the recorded sequence above the prediction, with time progressing from left to right. The leftmost column is the conditioning frame. The video generator uses one denoising step and ground-truth future object masks.

Fig. 5. Real-world evaluation setups. We evaluate TrajWAM on (a) conveyorbelt grasping with linear motion and (b) rotating-disc grasping with rotational motion. Both setups use two 6-DoF AgileX Piper arms, each equipped with a wrist-mounted Intel RealSense D435i camera, and a static D435i camera providing a global third-person view.

Fig. 1. Motivation and performance comparison. (a) Existing WAMs may fail to accurately anticipate target-object motion, resulting in future predictions that deviate from the actual trajectory. TrajWAM uses predicted future object masks as trajectory guidance to generate motion-consistent futures for action prediction. (b) Success rate and inference latency on DOMINO. TrajWAM achieves state-of-the-art performance while maintaining efficient inference.

Fig. 10. Video predictions for real-world dynamic grasping. The first three examples show conveyor-belt grasping with a banana, a bottle, and a roll of tape; the last two show rotating-disc grasping with a plush toy and a banana. Each pair of rows compares the recorded sequence with the prediction at corresponding time points, ordered from left to right.

papers.title: TrajWAM: An Efficient Trajectory-Guided World Action Model for Dynamic Robotic Manipulation
papers.tldr: TrajWAM improves dynamic robotic manipulation by explicitly predicting target-object trajectories to guide visual forecasting and fast one-step action generation.
